blocks.content: Aggregate Functions briefly mentioned that COUNT star and COUNT with a column name behave differently around NULL, without fully explaining why. COUNT versus COUNT star returns to that distinction directly, since it is genuinely common enough, and subtle enough, to deserve its own focused topic.

This topic covers exactly what each form actually counts, a worked example showing the difference produce genuinely different numbers on the same table, how COUNT DISTINCT fits into this picture, and a practical performance note worth knowing.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784035656018-396045983.png
blocks.alt: COUNT versus COUNT star covers a genuinely common, subtle distinction worth understanding precisely, not just stylistically

blocks.content: 1. The Two Forms

COUNT star counts every single row, regardless of whether any particular column in that row happens to be NULL. It is genuinely counting the existence of rows themselves, not evaluating any specific column value at all.

COUNT with a specific column name counts only the non NULL values present in that particular column, genuinely skipping any row where that specific column happens to be NULL, even though the row itself still exists and would have been counted by COUNT star.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784035657883-635751663.png
blocks.alt: COUNT star counts every row regardless of NULL; COUNT with a column name counts only non NULL values in that specific column

blocks.content: {"headers":["Form","What It Actually Counts"],"rows":[["COUNT star","Every row, regardless of any NULL values present"],["COUNT column","Only rows where that specific column is not NULL"]]}
2. A Worked Example

A concrete table shows this distinction producing genuinely different numbers. An employees table has a manager_id column, but some employees, likely senior leadership with no manager above them, genuinely have NULL in that specific column.

SELECT COUNT(*) FROM employees;
SELECT COUNT(manager_id) FROM employees;
blocks.code:
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM employees;
SELECT COUNT(manager_id) FROM employees;

codes.sql:
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM employees;
SELECT COUNT(manager_id) FROM employees;

blocks.content: COUNT star returns the total employee count, every single row in the table. COUNT manager_id returns only the employees who genuinely have a real, non NULL manager id, a smaller number, since it excludes anyone with no manager recorded.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784035659499-135131585.png
blocks.alt: A worked example: an employees table where COUNT star returns the total count, and COUNT manager_id returns only employees with a real manager

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.content: Assuming COUNT star and COUNT with a specific column name always return the same number. They genuinely only match when that specific column has no NULL values at all, which is not guaranteed for most real, genuinely optional columns.
3. Why This Difference Genuinely Matters

Assuming both forms return the same number is genuinely wrong whenever the relevant column actually contains any NULL values, which is a genuinely common situation for optional fields, a manager id, a discount code, a middle name.

Understanding the real difference deliberately means choosing the specific form that actually answers your real question, do you want the total number of rows that exist, or specifically the number of rows where a particular piece of information is genuinely present.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784035661328-117765739.png
blocks.alt: Assuming both forms match is genuinely wrong whenever the column contains NULL; understanding the real difference means choosing the form that actually answers your question

blocks.content: 4. COUNT Combined With DISTINCT

COUNT combined with DISTINCT counts only the unique, non NULL values present in that column, collapsing repeated values down before counting, and still genuinely excluding NULL entirely from the result.

COUNT DISTINCT customer_id on an orders table genuinely counts unique customers who placed at least one order, not the total number of orders, since a single customer placing many orders still only counts once toward this specific result.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784035662907-788171167.png
blocks.alt: COUNT combined with DISTINCT counts only unique, non NULL values, like counting unique customers rather than total orders

blocks.title: Worth remembering
blocks.content: COUNT DISTINCT genuinely excludes NULL just like a plain COUNT with a column name does. A NULL value never counts as a genuine, distinct value in either form.
5. A Practical Performance Note

COUNT star is often genuinely the fastest form to compute, in many real database implementations, since it never actually needs to check individual column values for NULL at all, it simply counts the existence of rows themselves.

COUNT with a specific column name genuinely requires checking each row for whether that column is NULL, which can carry a real, if usually small, additional cost compared to the simpler row existence check COUNT star performs.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784035664476-229140869.png
blocks.alt: COUNT star is often the fastest form since it never checks individual column values for NULL, unlike COUNT with a column name

blocks.content: 6. Genuinely Common Mistakes

A few real patterns undermine this distinction in practice. Assuming COUNT star and COUNT column always return the same number, which is genuinely wrong whenever that column contains any NULL values. Using COUNT column when you genuinely meant to count every row, silently undercounting because of NULL values you may not have anticipated.

And forgetting that COUNT DISTINCT also genuinely excludes NULL entirely, which can silently produce a smaller number than expected if the column has NULL values mixed in with genuinely meaningful ones.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784035665993-403074214.png
blocks.alt: Common mistakes: assuming both forms always match, using COUNT column when you meant every row, and forgetting COUNT DISTINCT also excludes NULL

Using COUNT column when you actually want every row counted: use COUNT star instead to count rows unconditionally.
Forgetting COUNT DISTINCT excludes NULL too: a NULL value never counts as a distinct value in either form.
